doc.title: Ann Rabson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 21, 2007

title: Called Jazzbo: bop, Bo Diddley, Little Richard and Mary Lou Williams records
summary: Her tastes set her apart from classmates; she loved bop and early rock and roll, and the family 78s of Mary Lou Williams shaped her and her jazz-pianist brother.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Were your tastes usually not aligned with the kids who were your age?

Absolutely. Absolutely. When I was in seventh grade they dubbed me “Jazzbo,” and they made fun of me. Well I loved jazz. I’ve always, I still love jazz. And I was listening to bop. I mean I was just really into that. But I was also, you know I was very lucky because the popular music when I was coming up was pretty cool, some of it. And I really loved Bo Diddley and Little Richard and you know people like that, Ruth Brown.
Were you a word person when you listened to the music? Did you really pay attention to the words?

No I really didn’t. And I think part of that comes from my jazz roots which are really not vocal roots. My father, my family had all kinds of music. No blues in our — uh that came later with me. But I remember we had like Mary Lou Williams — 78s — that was what was records when I was a kid. And you could hear her music in my music and you can hear her music in my brother’s playing. My brother is a jazz pianist, doesn’t play any blues, and I’m a blues pianist, don’t play any jazz, and you can hear Mary Lou Williams, her early work, this is when she was a boogie woogie person out of Kansas City.
